triage.name: Refeeding syndrome
triage.reason: Electrolyte derangement after refeeding a malnourished patient; a student can reach it from the feeding history and metabolic labs.

age.peak: adults with severe malnutrition; any age when starvation is prolonged

demographics: Occurs in anyone who has been severely malnourished and is then refed, so the age and sex distribution follows the underlying cause rather than the syndrome itself
Seen more often in hospitalized or institutionalized patients than in the community

risk_factors.text: Very low body weight or recent large unintentional weight loss
Little or no food intake for many days, including prolonged fasting or starvation
Low baseline levels of phosphate, potassium or magnesium before feeding is started
Anorexia nervosa or other severe eating disorder
Recent major surgery, critical illness or prolonged intensive care stay
Cancer or cancer treatment causing poor intake
Prolonged unconsciousness or inability to eat, such as after a stroke
Older age with frailty and poor oral intake

comorbidities: Anorexia nervosa or other eating disorder
Malabsorption syndromes such as celiac disease or chronic pancreatitis
social_history: Food insecurity or inability to afford food
Living alone with limited help preparing meals
Incarceration or other setting with restricted food access
exposures: Prolonged hospitalization or intensive care with little or no nutrition
Prolonged fasting for a medical procedure or religious reason
Recent start of tube feeding, intravenous nutrition or a large oral meal after a period of starvation

chief_complaints.text: I've been feeling weak and shaky since they started feeding me again
My heart feels like it's racing or skipping
My hands and feet are tingling
I've had watery diarrhea since the feeds started
I feel like I might pass out when I stand up

hpi.onset: Gradual, beginning within the first few days after eating or feeding is restarted following a period of poor intake or starvation
hpi.progression: Starts with vague weakness and malaise, then progresses to palpitations, confusion, muscle cramps and swelling as electrolyte levels fall; can worsen quickly to seizures, heart failure or arrhythmia if feeding continues unchanged
hpi.location: Generalized; swelling usually in the legs and sometimes the face
hpi.quality: Weakness and shakiness with a fluttering or racing heartbeat; muscle twitching and cramping
hpi.severity: Mild at first, then moderate to severe; can become life-threatening
hpi.timing: Worst in the first 5 days after refeeding starts
aggravating: Continuing or increasing the amount of food or tube feeds
relieving: Electrolyte replacement given by the care team

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the legs or ankles
Tingling in the hands and feet

pertinent_negatives: New focal weakness or one-sided numbness
Known heart disease before this admission

argues_against: Active infection as the cause of the weakness

positives.text: Swelling of the legs or ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Tingling in the hands and feet

argues_against: Primary psychiatric illness causing the symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and children may show irritability, poor feeding, lethargy and failure to thrive rather than describing palpitations or tingling; seizures and heart failure can appear quickly.
May present with falls, delirium or worsening heart failure rather than reporting specific symptoms; electrolyte drops can be missed if not checked.
Severe nausea and vomiting of pregnancy or hyperemesis can cause malnutrition and then refeeding syndrome; symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy complaints such as nausea, fatigue and swelling.
Kidneys handle phosphate and potassium poorly, so levels can swing faster and electrolyte replacement must be adjusted; edema and shortness of breath may be blamed on kidney disease.
Confusion may be attributed to liver disease rather than low phosphate or magnesium, and low albumin can mask the degree of malnutrition.

general.mild: Thin, tired-appearing but alert and conversant; able to sit up without help
general.moderate: Markedly cachectic, weak, slow to move; needs help sitting up; looks unwell
general.severe: Severely wasted, ill-appearing, drowsy or agitated; too weak to sit unaided
general.critical: Cachectic and obtunded or in respiratory distress; pale, clammy, barely responsive

findings.finding: Sunken temples with loss of subcutaneous fat

findings.finding: Dry, tacky oral mucosa

findings.finding: Jugular venous distension

Dry, flaky skin with poor turgor
Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound

labs.caveat: Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark; it develops within 1-3 days of starting feeds and may be masked if not checked daily.
Hypokalemia from insulin-driven intracellular shift; worsens arrhythmia risk.
Hypomagnesemia must be corrected or potassium and phosphate replacement will not hold.
Hyponatremia from water retention and antidiuretic hormone effect during refeeding.
Carbohydrate load causes hyperglycemia and drives insulin release, which precipitates the electrolyte shifts.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from diarrhea or underlying illness.
Hypocalcemia often accompanies hypomagnesemia and can cause tetany or seizures.
Low albumin reflects malnutrition and lowers total calcium; use ionized calcium when albumin is low.
More reliable than total calcium in hypoalbuminemia.
Elevated from dehydration and poor intake before refeeding.
May be falsely reassuring in severe malnutrition because low muscle mass lowers baseline creatinine.
Anemia from malnutrition or underlying disease; may be masked by dehydration until fluids are given.
Thrombocytopenia can occur with severe malnutrition, alcohol use or folate deficiency.
Leukopenia suggests severe malnutrition or concurrent infection; a normal or low count does not exclude infection.
Deficiency is common in the malnourished and contributes to anemia and neuropathy.
Low folate is common with poor intake and alcohol use.
Sick euthyroid pattern or hypothyroidism can accompany severe malnutrition and mimic the fatigue.
Ketones reflect starvation before refeeding and should clear as carbohydrate is given.

Prolonged QT interval
ST depression or flattened T waves
Flattened or inverted T waves
Premature atrial or ventricular beats
Ventricular tachycardia or torsades de pointes
Prolonged PR interval or atrioventricular block
U waves from hypokalemia

findings.text: Pulmonary edema or pleural effusions from fluid overload
Enlarged cardiac silhouette suggesting heart failure

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected heart failure, arrhythmia or unexplained dyspnea

The hallmark abnormality; check before refeeding and daily for the first several days
Anemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia reflect the severity of malnutrition and screen for infection
Hyperglycemia from the carbohydrate load drives the electrolyte shifts
Assesses nutritional status and helps interpret total calcium
Detects QT prolongation and arrhythmias from low potassium, magnesium and calcium
initial.only_if: palpitations, syncope or severe electrolyte derangement

confirmatory.why: Falling potassium with refeeding supports the diagnosis

supporting.why: Clarifies calcium status when albumin is low
Identifies a treatable deficiency contributing to the malnutrition
Identifies a treatable deficiency contributing to the malnutrition
Excludes hypothyroidism as an alternative cause of fatigue and edema
Looks for pulmonary edema or effusions from fluid overload
supporting.only_if: dyspnea, crackles or suspected heart failure

supporting.why: Assesses ventricular function when heart failure or arrhythmia is suspected
supporting.only_if: suspected heart failure or new arrhythmia

not_indicated.why: No role; does not distinguish refeeding syndrome from its mimics
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis

decision_points: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium before starting feeds and daily for the first several days
Do not start or advance nutrition until electrolytes are corrected in a high-risk patient
A falling phosphate after refeeding begins confirms the diagnosis
Correct magnesium first or potassium and phosphate replacement will not hold

criteria.name: Refeeding syndrome (clinical definition)
criteria.summary: Electrolyte and metabolic derangement occurring within the first five days of reintroducing nutrition in a malnourished patient, most often marked by a fall in phosphate, potassium or magnesium, with or without clinical symptoms.
items: Malnutrition or prolonged poor intake before refeeding
Fall in phosphate, potassium or magnesium within five days
May include thiamine deficiency, fluid overload and arrhythmia

differential.name: Hypophosphatemia from another cause
differential.why_considered: Low phosphate is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome, but many other conditions lower phosphate without any refeeding.
differential.trigger: Low phosphate without a clear refeeding trigger, or phosphate that stays low despite holding feeds

history: No period of starvation or malnutrition before the low phosphate
Alcohol use disorder with recent heavy drinking
Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation or sepsis
Use of phosphate-binding antacids or diuretics
exam: Signs of the underlying cause such as alcohol withdrawal or respiratory failure
labs: Low phosphate without a clear temporal link to starting feeds
Respiratory alkalosis on blood gas
Normal or high phosphate before nutrition was started

differential.name: Hypokalemia from another cause
differential.why_considered: Low potassium is common in refeeding syndrome but also occurs with diuretics, vomiting and diarrhea.
differential.trigger: Low potassium with metabolic alkalosis or a clear non-nutritional cause

history: Diuretic use or recent increase in dose
Vomiting or diarrhea before refeeding
No clear period of starvation
exam: Signs of volume depletion such as dry mucosa and low jugular venous pressure
Muscle weakness out of proportion to the feeding history
labs: Metabolic alkalosis suggesting vomiting or diuretics
Low potassium without a fall in phosphate
Urine potassium helps separate renal from gastrointestinal losses
ecg: U waves and flattened T waves from hypokalemia

differential.name: Hypomagnesemia from another cause
differential.why_considered: Low magnesium is part of refeeding syndrome but also occurs with alcohol use, diarrhea and proton pump inhibitors.

history: Chronic alcohol use
Chronic diarrhea or malabsorption
Long-term proton pump inhibitor use
exam: Tetany, Chvostek sign or Trousseau sign
labs: Low magnesium without a fall in phosphate
Low calcium that corrects only after magnesium is replaced
Low magnesium before nutrition was restarted

differential.name: Thiamine deficiency (Wernicke encephalopathy)
differential.why_considered: Thiamine deficiency often coexists with refeeding syndrome in malnourished patients and can be unmasked by giving carbohydrate.
differential.trigger: Confusion, ataxia or eye movement abnormalities after carbohydrate is given to a malnourished patient

history: Heavy alcohol use or poor intake for weeks
Confusion and unsteadiness that worsen after a glucose load
No palpitations or edema
exam: Confusion with a relatively normal cardiovascular exam
labs: Low phosphate may be absent
Normal potassium and magnesium in some cases

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Hyperglycemia, dehydration and electrolyte shifts can mimic the metabolic picture of refeeding syndrome.
differential.trigger: High glucose with ketones and metabolic acidosis

history: Known diabetes or polyuria and polydipsia
Nausea and vomiting before any refeeding
No period of starvation
labs: High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Positive serum or urine ketones
Glucose often above 250 mg/dL

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Edema, dyspnea and crackles in refeeding syndrome can be mistaken for heart failure, and the two can coexist.

history: Known heart disease or prior heart failure
Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea before refeeding
No clear malnutrition or starvation
exam: S3 gallop and displaced apical impulse
labs: Elevated BNP or NT-proBNP
Normal phosphate and magnesium
imaging: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema or pleural effusions on chest x-ray

differential.name: Sepsis
differential.why_considered: Fever, tachycardia, confusion and hypotension can overlap with severe refeeding syndrome.
differential.trigger: Fever, hypotension and a source of infection

history: Fever and chills before refeeding
Recent infection, surgery or indwelling line
No clear period of starvation
exam: Fever, hypotension and warm or cold extremities
Localizing signs such as cough, dysuria or line site redness
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia
Elevated lactate
Normal phosphate in early sepsis
imaging: Infiltrate on chest x-ray or source found on CT

differential.name: Alcohol withdrawal
differential.why_considered: Tremor, confusion, tachycardia and electrolyte abnormalities in a malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder can mimic refeeding syndrome.

history: Last drink within the past few days
Tremor, sweating and anxiety that worsen over hours
Prior withdrawal seizures
exam: Normal phosphate and magnesium in some cases
labs: Elevated AST and ALT with an AST/ALT ratio above 2
Macrocytosis
Electrolyte abnormalities may be present but do not track with feeding

severity.mild: Electrolyte levels fall modestly after refeeding begins, with weakness and fatigue but no arrhythmia, confusion or edema; patient is alert and able to eat.
severity.moderate: Clear hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia with palpitations, muscle cramps, pitting edema or mild confusion; needs close monitoring and electrolyte replacement.
severity.severe: Marked electrolyte derangement with arrhythmia, heart failure, marked confusion or seizure; requires intensive monitoring and slowing or holding feeds.
severity.critical: Life-threatening arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock, respiratory failure or status epilepticus from severe electrolyte derangement; needs ICU care and immediate electrolyte replacement.

red_flags.meaning: Arrhythmia from low potassium, magnesium or calcium; check ECG and electrolytes now
Severe electrolyte derangement or thiamine deficiency; give thiamine and check phosphate, magnesium and calcium
Cardiovascular compromise from arrhythmia, heart failure or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Rapidly worsening edema or shortness of breath
red_flags.meaning: Fluid overload and heart failure from aggressive refeeding
Severe hypophosphatemia with risk of arrhythmia, heart failure and rhabdomyolysis

red_flags.finding: Potassium below 2.5 mmol/L or magnesium below 1.0 mg/dL
red_flags.meaning: High risk of arrhythmia; replace magnesium first or potassium will not hold

complications.name: Rhabdomyolysis
clues: Dark urine with elevated creatine kinase

complications.name: Wernicke encephalopathy
clues: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus after carbohydrate is given
Heavy alcohol use or prolonged poor intake

complications.name: Respiratory failure
clues: Rising carbon dioxide on blood gas

special_populations.differences: Infants and children may show irritability, lethargy, poor feeding and failure to thrive rather than describing palpitations or tingling; seizures and heart failure can appear quickly, so electrolytes are checked more often.
May present with falls, delirium or worsening heart failure rather than specific symptoms; electrolyte drops can be missed if not checked, and fluid overload is more likely with aggressive refeeding.

Severe nausea and vomiting of pregnancy or hyperemesis can cause malnutrition and then refeeding syndrome; symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy complaints such as nausea, fatigue and swelling, so a clear temporal link to refeeding is important.

Kidneys handle phosphate and potassium poorly, so levels can swing faster and electrolyte replacement must be adjusted; edema and shortness of breath may be blamed on kidney disease rather than refeeding.
Confusion may be attributed to liver disease rather than low phosphate or magnesium, and low albumin can mask the degree of malnutrition.
Uncontrolled diabetes with poor intake increases risk; hyperglycemia from refeeding can be mistaken for poor diabetes control, and insulin drives potassium and phosphate into cells.

key_questions.question: How much have you been eating over the past one to two weeks, and for how many days have you been eating little or nothing?
key_questions.looking_for: A clear period of prolonged poor intake or starvation before nutrition was restarted

key_questions.question: When did you start eating or get started on tube feeds or IV nutrition again?
key_questions.looking_for: Nutrition restarted within the past 1–5 days, which is the typical window for refeeding syndrome

key_questions.question: How much and how fast have the feeds been increased since they started?
key_questions.looking_for: Aggressive or rapid advancement of calories or carbohydrate, which precipitates the electrolyte shifts

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weakness, shakiness or feeling like your heart is racing or skipping?
key_questions.looking_for: Weakness and palpitations from hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia

key_questions.question: Have you had any confusion, tingling in the hands and feet, or muscle cramps or twitching?
key_questions.looking_for: Neuromuscular irritability from low magnesium, calcium or phosphate

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your legs or ankles, or new shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluid overload and heart failure from aggressive refeeding

key_questions.question: Have you had any watery diarrhea since the feeds started?
key_questions.looking_for: Diarrhea, which worsens electrolyte losses and is part of the syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any seizures or times when you passed out?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizure or syncope from severe electrolyte derangement, which requires urgent treatment

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of an eating disorder, alcohol use disorder, cancer or recent major surgery or critical illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that cause severe malnutrition and put the patient at high risk

key_questions.question: Have you been on insulin, diuretics such as furosemide or hydrochlorothiazide, or steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that drive electrolytes into cells or cause renal losses, worsening the derangement

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble affording food or preparing meals, or been in a setting with limited food access?
key_questions.looking_for: Food insecurity or restricted access that explains the malnutrition

key_questions.question: Have you been vomiting or having diarrhea or trouble absorbing food before the feeds started?
key_questions.looking_for: Gastrointestinal losses that lower baseline electrolytes and raise risk

reasoning_points: A clear period of prolonged poor intake or starvation before nutrition was restarted
Nutrition restarted or advanced within the past 1–5 days
Falling phosphate, potassium or magnesium after refeeding began, with hypophosphatemia as the hallmark
Symptoms of weakness, palpitations, confusion, paresthesia, cramps or edema tracking with the refeeding
Risk factors such as low body weight, alcohol use disorder, eating disorder, cancer or critical illness
Alternative causes of isolated electrolyte abnormalities excluded, such as diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, sepsis or diabetic ketoacidosis
Thiamine deficiency considered and treated in a malnourished patient with confusion or neurologic findings

easy: Clear history of prolonged starvation followed by restarting feeds
Classic hypophosphatemia with weakness and palpitations within the first few days
Obvious risk factor such as anorexia nervosa or alcohol use disorder
Electrolytes checked before and after refeeding show a clear fall
medium: Older adult with frailty and poor intake who develops falls, delirium or worsening edema rather than classic symptoms
Patient on diuretics whose hypokalemia is blamed on the medication rather than refeeding
Hyperglycemia from the carbohydrate load mistaken for poor diabetes control
Symptoms overlap with heart failure or sepsis, requiring careful separation
hard: Patient with renal impairment where phosphate and potassium swing quickly and replacement must be adjusted
Confusion attributed to hepatic encephalopathy or alcohol withdrawal rather than low phosphate or magnesium
Pregnancy with hyperemesis and malnutrition where nausea, fatigue and swelling overlap with normal pregnancy complaints
Thiamine deficiency unmasked by carbohydrate with confusion, ataxia and nystagmus but minimal electrolyte change
Normal or near-normal phosphate because levels were not checked before refeeding or were masked by other illness
